graphEvents.label: Anthropic rejected semantic indexing for Claude Code and recommends agentic search first
Built-in agent search is lexical plus LSP; none ships a semantic index
Independent measurements show a conditional retrieval gain on large or noisy codebases
Independent evidence supports a cost thesis but not an accuracy thesis
No independent party has measured sweet-search itself

label: The maker of Claude Code tried semantic indexing for code search, rejected it, and still recommends starting with agentic search; index drift and index-hosting security liability were named reasons.

Codex bundles ripgrep and fuzzy file search, OpenCode ships ripgrep grep/glob plus an LSP tool with definition, reference, workspace-symbol and call-hierarchy operations, and Claude Code is documented as agentic search; none of the three ships a semantic index, so sweet-search differentiates on hybrid ranking rather than on search capability.

Independent measurements support a real but conditional retrieval gain concentrated on large or lexically noisy codebases: Cursor reports 12.5% average accuracy over grep, CodeRAG-Bench puts dense retrieval ahead of BM25 at repository level (46.4-67.4 versus 43), a structural-index ablation moves resolve from 41.9% to 50.4%, and an LSP-versus-grep pilot finds the gain flips with lexical noise (+0.000 F1 on a clean repo versus +0.246 on a noisy one).

Independent evidence undercuts an accuracy thesis and supports only a cost or latency thesis: an Augment-built SWE-bench agent found grep and find sufficient, a semantic-index vendor reports 92.0% accuracy both with and without its index while cutting tokens to the first right file from 15,491 to 224, and the LSP pilot shows semantic tools costing tokens on symbol-named localization and losing to grep on multi-file renames (67% versus 100%).

No independent party has measured sweet-search, and the closest analogues differ in the two variables that drive the gain, embedding-model quality and index lifecycle; Cursor trains a model on agent traces and documents a five-minute sync plus unavailability until 80% of indexing completes, so sweet-search's magnitude stays unverified while its direction is plausible.

direction: Treating Cursor's 12.5% accuracy figure as transferable to sweet-search
reason: Cursor attributes the gain to an embedding model trained on its own agent traces, so the number describes that model rather than local embeddings in general.

direction: Treating Anthropic's reversal as proof that no code index can help
reason: The published reasons are maintenance, transparency, accuracy and index-hosting liability for their own product; they do not measure third-party indexes against their harness.

direction: Using CodeRAG-Bench and the structural-index ablation as direct support for sweet-search
reason: Both evaluate retrieval or localisation components rather than sweet-search's tool contract, and CodeRAG-Bench's repository slice is document retrieval for generation rather than agentic tool use.
